synopsis: WNM-3D converts monocular observation history into geometry-aware tokens that condition a shared diffusion transformer generating future visual latents and navigation actions. Deployment executes the first action block, observes the simulator again, and replans; generated images never replace observations. Its GN-Bench results support improved simulated navigation over an RGB-history counterpart. Curriculum ablations show that DAgger increases success, while subsequent reward refinement improves path efficiency; applying reward refinement directly after offline supervision instead degrades success. [E05, E07, E15, E16]

problem.text: The authors argue that action-centric VLN training leaves observation changes under predicted motion insufficiently constrained. Existing navigation WAMs couple future observations and actions but lack an explicit mechanism for consolidating monocular history into shared geometry-aware conditioning. WNM-3D addresses this representation problem alongside the distribution shift caused by executing imperfect policies.

contributions.text: A navigation WAM uses geometry-aware history tokens as a clean inference-time condition shared by future-view and action generation.

A Scene-to-Token Adapter bridges frozen VGGT-Ω features and the DiT interface using location-dependent feature fusion, content-initialized queries, anchored deformable resampling, and spatial–temporal refinement.
A three-stage curriculum combines expert supervision, policy-state correction, and Counterfactual DanceGRPO with localized denoising interventions and modality-specific reward routing.

inputs: Language instruction, current egocentric RGB observation, and 33 RGB history frames sampled uniformly over the observed trajectory. [E07, E08]
No depth, camera pose, BEV observation, or explicit metric map is supplied to the deployed policy. Simulator pose supports action execution and reward computation outside the policy input. [E08, E09]
Training supervision includes A* actions and corresponding rendered futures; Stage-III records additionally contain occupancy information and navigation metadata. [E10, E11]
outputs: Future visual latents corresponding to 32 RGB frames and 32 aligned motion increments, partitioned into four blocks of eight frames/actions. [E08]
Each physical action contains planar translation and yaw increments; at most the first eight actions are executed before replanning. [E03, E18]

steps.name: Construct the scene prefix
steps.detail: Frozen VGGT-Ω processes history at 512×512. The adapter fuses four encoder levels at corresponding history-patch locations, pools a coarse target lattice, and adds learned slots and structured embeddings. Two anchored resampling layers retrieve local detail; two factorized spatial–temporal blocks refine it. Detail and coarse residual heads produce 450 tokens of width 3072, matching WNM-2D's prefix interface.

steps.name: Connect history and paired future blocks
steps.detail: The clean prefix enters DiT self-attention, while current-image and language encodings supply native cross-attention context. Within each temporal block, visual and action tokens interact bidirectionally. They can access the prefix, block zero, and preceding blocks, but cannot access later blocks. The prefix itself attends only within the prefix.

steps.name: Learn coupled velocity fields
steps.detail: A frozen video VAE encodes visual targets. Actions are scaled, quantile-normalized, and padded to the backbone's fixed width. Paired visual/action blocks share a flow timestep but receive independent noise. Separate modality transformations and output heads surround the shared DiT, which predicts both velocity fields.

steps.name: Decode motion in a fixed local frame
steps.detail: The first three action dimensions are inverse-normalized and divided by the training scale. All XY increments retain the coordinate axes of the current camera-anchored frame. Their cumulative translation is transformed to world coordinates; accumulated yaw does not recursively rotate subsequent XY increments.

training.text: Stage-I trains for 20 epochs on 16K A* demonstrations. A sampled replanning state receives expert actions and simulator-rendered future observations along that same trajectory.

Stage-II rolls each Stage-I policy out on the same 16K tasks, queries expert corrections at visited states, and renders matching corrective futures. Five supervised epochs use approximately 633K WNM-3D chunks or 691K WNM-2D chunks.

Stage-III starts from Stage-II and approximately 96K fixed records recollected using that policy. Current-policy samples are scored against stored annotations without stepping the interactive simulator. There is no auxiliary supervised world-action loss.

Four denoising strata each supply one intervention transition. Four branches share initial latents and all other SDE noise, producing 16 completed samples per condition. Rewards use complete samples, but gradients replay only the intervened transition. Advantages are standardized within each condition–stratum group; visual credit uses visual transition ratios, while navigation and stopping credit use action-chunk ratios.

Visual rewards combine reconstruction, temporal consistency, pyramid-averaged SSIM, degradation penalties, and a small optical-flow/action consistency bonus. A fixed ridge regressor calibrated on 480 reference clips estimates motion; its yaw estimate is diagnostic only. Navigation rewards score progress, route adherence, collisions, and orientation. Stopping rewards encourage settling inside the goal region and penalize unsuccessful STOP or departure.

inference.text: At every replan, history is resampled and its prefix recomputed. Visual and action variables are jointly sampled from Gaussian noise. Only the first action block is executed, and newly acquired simulator observations extend history. Predicted visual latents are neither decoded to RGB nor inserted into history.

STOP occurs before execution when first-block XY path length is strictly below 0.15 m. Otherwise, actions are inspected in order; an action whose three absolute components are all at most 10^-3 stops execution before that action.

equations.explanation: Equation (3): the frozen geometry encoder E_geo transforms observed history H_t; trainable adapter T_ϕ produces the clean conditioning prefix. Its geometry is represented through learned features, without requiring a metric map as policy input.

Equation (5): modality m is visual or action, and b denotes a temporal block. The interpolation joins data to Gaussian noise; the DiT learns its velocity. Aligned modalities share σ_b but not their noise samples.

equations.expression: L_WA = E[MSE_w(û^v,u^v) + λ_a MSE_{w,M_a}(û^a,u^a)], with λ_a = 1.
equations.explanation: Equation (6): supervised training combines timestep-weighted visual and action velocity errors. M_a zeros residuals in padded action dimensions; the shifted discrete schedule and unit-mean weights are specified in Equations (16)–(17).

equations.expression: A^q_{i,k,h} = (R^q_{i,k,h}−μ^q_{i,k})/(σ^q_{i,k}+ϵ); L_III = L_v + λ_act(L_nav + λ_stop L_stop).
equations.explanation: Equations (10) and (12): reward stream q is normalized across counterfactual branches h within condition i and stratum k. Clipped modality-routed surrogates form the losses. The implementation uses λ_act=0.25, λ_stop=0.50, navigation chunk weights (8,4,2,1)/15, and uniform stopping-loss averaging.

results.setting: GN-Bench Seen; 1,000 simulator episodes; full three-stage models; inference seed 1140.
results.comparison: WNM-2D: 75.6 SR, 72.9 SPL. GN-BAE with additional BEV observations: 58.6 SR, 58.6 SPL.
results.interpretation: Analysis: gains over WNM-2D are 13.1 and 8.0 percentage points. These measure executed simulator navigation, not generated-video quality. Comparisons with prior methods do not establish matched training data or compute.

results.setting: GN-Bench Unseen; 5,000 simulator episodes; full three-stage models; inference seed 1140.
results.comparison: WNM-2D: 45.9 SR, 42.8 SPL. FPV-only GN-BAE: 38.9 SR, 37.3 SPL.
results.interpretation: Analysis: WNM-3D gains 7.6 SR and 3.8 SPL points over its counterpart, and 14.6 SR and 9.3 SPL points over FPV-only GN-BAE. The paper explicitly cautions that these results do not show a reduced Seen-to-Unseen gap.

results.task: Effect of supervised correction at policy-visited states
results.setting: WNM-3D Stage-II versus Stage-I; identical GN-Bench evaluation episodes and inference procedure.
results.value: Stage-II: Seen SR 80.7, SPL 66.6; Unseen SR 49.7, SPL 38.2, TL 13.2.
results.comparison: Stage-I: Seen SR 56.7, SPL 54.4; Unseen SR 43.1, SPL 41.6, TL 5.9.
results.interpretation: Analysis: DAgger improves success on both splits, but unseen SPL falls while trajectories lengthen. Expert correction therefore does not independently guarantee efficient navigation under scene shift.

results.task: Effect of reward refinement after DAgger
results.setting: WNM-3D Stage-III versus Stage-II on the same evaluation protocol.
results.metric: Changes in SR and SPL, in percentage points; reported TL
results.value: Seen: +8.0 SR, +14.3 SPL; Unseen: +3.8 SR, +8.4 SPL.
results.comparison: TL decreases from 13.9 to 10.6 on Seen and from 13.2 to 10.2 on Unseen.
results.interpretation: Analysis: reward refinement improves both success and efficiency from the adapted checkpoint. This stage comparison does not isolate counterfactual sampling from its reward design or other optimization choices.

results.setting: WNM-3D initialized from Stage-I; direct DanceGRPO uses records from the same Stage-I-policy collection underlying DAgger.
results.interpretation: Analysis: direct reward refinement degrades success in this tested configuration. This supports the curriculum choice, while the proposed explanation involving poor counterfactual diversity and reward separation remains unmeasured.

limitations.text: Evidence is restricted to GN-Bench simulation. Each checkpoint is evaluated once per episode with one inference seed; no multi-seed variability or bootstrap intervals are reported. Physical-robot performance and statistical reliability across training runs remain unestablished.

WNM-2D matches the backbone and 450-token interface, but the comparison also introduces a pretrained geometry encoder, higher-resolution processing, and additional adapter parameters. Policy-specific DAgger datasets and batch sizes differ. Tables 1–2 do not isolate geometry from these factors or ablate individual adapter components.

The authors hypothesize that DAgger produces stronger policy support for reward refinement, whereas Stage-I counterfactual groups may be uniformly poor or weakly differentiated. They acknowledge that action-diversity and reward-spread measurements are needed to verify this mechanism.

Stage-III evaluates generated futures against fixed reference observations and actions against stored trajectory and occupancy information. This supplies useful training signals but does not directly verify that generated videos match the environment's response to each sampled action sequence. The optical-flow bonus checks translation agreement and excludes yaw from its reward.

The experimental tables establish navigation outcomes, not a separate quantitative improvement in predictive visual dynamics. There is also no reported latency or compute-matched deployment comparison, despite recomputing geometry features at every replan.

reproduction.text: Required components include Wan2.2-TI2V-5B initialization, frozen VGGT-Ω, the specified adapter, GN-Bench simulation, A* supervision, and policy-specific data collection. Stages I–II use 16 H100 GPUs, AdamW at initial learning rate 10^-5, and global batches of 192 for WNM-3D versus 256 for WNM-2D.

Stage-III specifies 1,500 AdamW updates at learning rate 5×10^-6, condition batch 64, a 16-transition sampler, and CFG scale 5. Reproduction must preserve intervention strata, reward routing, chunk weights, occupancy handling, and the strict ordered STOP detector; these details determine the optimization target.

Checkpoint-associated action quantiles are required but their numerical values are absent. Trajectory smoothing and temporal sampling are not fully specified. Table 8 describes Stage-III sampling; the text does not separately establish all deployment sampler settings. These are concrete implementation gaps to resolve before claiming faithful reproduction.

A focused mechanism test would compare scene-prefix alternatives using identical correction records and controlled image resolution and compute. A separate Stage-II-initialized comparison against ordinary DanceGRPO should match generated-sample budgets and record reward spread and action diversity.
The title page links code and model artifacts. Their contents and availability were not inspected, and no experiments were reproduced in this review.

reasoning.text: The supplied Q1 classification is supported by architecture evidence: one shared world-action DiT predicts both visual and action velocity fields, with bidirectional interaction inside aligned blocks and joint sampling at inference. Separate modality heads and a frozen geometry conditioner do not constitute a separate inverse-dynamics action policy. Navigation and multiview geometry conditioning are directly supported, although the scene representation consists of learned history-patch features rather than an explicit metric map.

discussionQuestions: How much of the geometry-prefix advantage remains with matched history resolution, compute, and corrective training records? [E08, E10, E15]
Does counterfactual denoising intervention outperform ordinary DanceGRPO at equal sampling cost, and do measured reward spread and action diversity explain the need for DAgger? [E11, E16]
Would action-conditioned simulator checks of generated futures reveal inconsistencies missed by fixed-reference visual rewards and translation-only flow agreement? [E11, E12]

evidence.location: PDF p. 1, title page and arXiv version line
evidence.detail: The supplied title, identifier, and ten authors match the catalog. The source identifies arXiv:2608.07267v2 dated 20 August 2026 and lists project, code, and model links.

The motivation concerns missing predictive constraints in action-centric policies, absent explicit geometry-aware history consolidation in existing navigation WAMs, and policy-induced distribution shift.

Targets are consecutive planar and wrapped tangent-heading increments of a smoothed trajectory, expressed in a fixed local frame anchored at the current camera pose. Simulator trajectory quantities construct targets rather than policy observations.

evidence.location: PDF p. 6, Section 3.4, Equations (7)–(9); p. 7, paragraph preceding Section 3.5
evidence.detail: The adapter performs per-location encoder-level fusion, pooled content initialization, structured query embedding, anchored local resampling, and factorized spatial–temporal refinement with a coarse residual. The geometry encoder remains frozen.

evidence.location: PDF p. 5, Section 3.2, Equations (3)–(4) and attention-mask description
evidence.detail: Clean scene tokens enter self-attention; image and language context enters cross-attention. Temporal-block masking permits paired visual/action interaction and access to prior blocks while excluding later blocks.

evidence.location: PDF p. 5, Section 3.3, Equations (5)–(6); p. 16, Section A.3, Equations (16)–(17)
evidence.detail: Visual and action variables share a DiT but retain separate transformations and heads. Paired blocks share timesteps with independent Gaussian noise. Training uses weighted velocity errors, masks padded action dimensions, and sets the action coefficient to one.

Each replan resamples observed history and recomputes conditioning. Jointly sampled visual/action futures yield execution of only the first action block. Predicted visual latents are not decoded or incorporated into observation history.

evidence.location: PDF pp. 14–15, Section A.1 and Table 3
evidence.detail: Configuration includes Wan2.2-TI2V-5B, 33 history frames, 160×320 backbone inputs, 512×512 geometry inputs, four blocks of eight future frames/actions, and matched 450-token prefixes of width 3072. VGGT-Ω levels 5, 12, 18, and 24 feed an adapter with two resampling and two refinement layers.

evidence.location: PDF p. 15, Section A.2, Equations (13)–(15) and ordered STOP description
evidence.detail: Actions use scale four, checkpoint-specific first/99th-percentile quantiles, and width-32 padding. Fixed-frame XY increments are rotated using the current camera frame independently of accumulated yaw. STOP uses strict chunk path length below 0.15 m or a componentwise 10^-3 threshold.

evidence.location: PDF pp. 15–16, Section A.3 and Table 4
evidence.detail: Stage-I uses 16K demonstrations for 20 epochs. Stage-II collects approximately 691K WNM-2D and 633K WNM-3D corrective chunks over the same 16K tasks and trains for five epochs. AdamW settings, 16 H100 GPUs, and respective global batches 256/192 are specified.

evidence.location: PDF pp. 7–8, Section 3.5, Equations (10)–(12); pp. 16–17, Sections A.4–A.4.1, Equations (18)–(20)
evidence.detail: Stage-III uses approximately 96K fixed annotated records without interactive simulator stepping or supervised loss. Full-curriculum records come from Stage-II; direct-refinement records come from the Stage-I collection. Four strata and four controlled-noise branches yield 16 samples per condition with intervention-only gradient replay and modality-routed clipped surrogates.

evidence.location: PDF pp. 17–19, Section A.4.2, Equations (21)–(30), Table 5
evidence.detail: Visual scoring combines pyramid-averaged SSIM, reconstruction, temporal differences, and degradation factors. A 0.05-weight flow bonus uses a fixed ridge regressor fitted on 480 reference clips, translation agreement or stationarity, and flow confidence; inferred yaw is excluded from the reward.

evidence.location: PDF pp. 19–20, Section A.4.3, Equations (31)–(36), Table 6; p. 15, collision-handling paragraph
evidence.detail: Navigation rewards combine geodesic progress, path-length agreement, goal potential and entry, collision penalties, route deviation, backward movement, and yaw consistency. Navigation-active and full raw-plan horizons differ; occupancy-based execution handling includes contact clipping.

evidence.location: PDF pp. 20–21, Section A.4.4, Equations (37)–(41), Table 7
evidence.detail: Stopping rewards combine goal-potential reduction, translation/rotation energy, hard STOP success or failure, and a goal-exit penalty. The configured goal radius is 1.5 m.

evidence.location: PDF pp. 9–10, Section 4.2; p. 10, Table 1, WNM-2D, WNM-3D, and GN-BAE rows
evidence.detail: Table 1 reports WNM-3D Seen SR/SPL 88.7/80.9 and Unseen 53.5/46.6; WNM-2D reports 75.6/72.9 and 45.9/42.8. GN-BAE with BEV reports Seen 58.6/58.6; FPV-only GN-BAE reports Unseen 38.9/37.3. Section 4.2 states that the Seen-to-Unseen gap is not reduced.

evidence.location: PDF pp. 10–11, Section 4.3; p. 11, Table 2, WNM-3D rows
evidence.detail: The narrative disambiguates the two-stage rows. Stage-I, Stage-II, direct DanceGRPO, and full-curriculum SR are respectively 56.7/80.7/47.1/88.7 Seen and 43.1/49.7/39.2/53.5 Unseen. Corresponding SPL and TL entries document the efficiency tradeoffs. The final paragraph identifies diversity and reward-spread explanations as unverified.

evidence.location: PDF p. 21, Section A.4.5, Equations (42)–(44); p. 22, Section A.4.6, Table 8
evidence.detail: Navigation losses use weights (8,4,2,1)/15 and stopping losses are averaged. Stage-III uses condition batch 64, 16 sampler transitions, CFG five, AdamW learning rate 5×10^-6, 1,500 updates, action weight 0.25, and stopping weight 0.50.

evidence.location: PDF p. 22, Section B.1 GN-Bench Closed-Loop Evaluation
evidence.detail: Seen and Unseen contain 1,000 and 5,000 episodes. Evaluation executes at most eight actions before replanning and applies the shared STOP rules. Each checkpoint is evaluated once per episode using seed 1140; reported results are point estimates without multi-seed standard deviations or bootstrap confidence intervals.
